Q: How can I specify the function type in my type hints? A:

The forms described in Dimitris Fasarakis Hilliard's answer work well for callables with a fixed number of positional arguments, as well as variadic callables where the parameter types won't be used later. You'll need different tools for more complicated cases.

TypeVarTuple

You can express variadic callables with preserved type information using a TypeVarTuple. This is like the Callable[..., R] form, but it doesn't discard the parameter types, so you can reuse them for other purposes. For example, the following function passes those parameter types to its return type:

from collections.abc import Callable


def preserve_signature[*Ts, R](func: Callable[[*Ts], R]) -> Callable[[*Ts], R]:
    return func

def foo(bar: int) -> bool:
    return True

def spam(ham: int, eggs: str) -> bool:
    return True


reveal_type(preserve_signature(foo)) # (int) -> bool
reveal_type(preserve_signature(spam)) # (int, str) -> bool

You can even chain *Ts to the end of an existing argument list to restrict the first several positional arguments; [int, str, *Ts] means "an int, a str, and any number of positional arguments, which will be preserved".

from collections.abc import Callable
from typing import Concatenate


def requires_int[*Ts, R](func: Callable[[int, str, *Ts], R]) -> Callable[[int, str, *Ts], R]:
    return func

def foo(bar: int, baz: str, quz: bool) -> None:
    return None

def spam(ham: str) -> None:
    return None


reveal_type(requires_int(foo)) # (int, str, bool) -> None
requires_int(spam) # Error

ParamSpec

TypeVarTuple discards parameter names and disallows keyword-only arguments. A ParamSpec removes both those restrictions. Notice how this "better" version of preserve_signature lets the type checker infer parameter names from the return type:

from collections.abc import Callable


def preserve_signature_better[**P, R](func: Callable[P, R]) -> Callable[P, R]:
    return func

def foo(bar: int, /, baz: str, *, quz: bool) -> None:
    return None


reveal_type(preserve_signature_better(foo)) # (bar: int, /, baz: str, *, quz: bool) -> None

You can even access the arguments and keyword arguments of a ParamSpec to annotate *args and **kwargs of other functions:

from collections.abc import Callable


def obfuscated[**P, R](func: Callable[P, R]) -> Callable[P, R]:
    def inner(*args: P.args, **kwargs: P.kwargs) -> R:
        return func(*args, **kwargs)
    return inner

def foo(bar: int, /, baz: str, *, quz: bool) -> None:
    return None


reveal_type(obfuscated(foo)) # (bar: int, /, baz: str, *, quz: bool) -> None

You can chain a ParamSpec to the end of an existing positional argument list, much like a TypeVarTuple, but you'll need Concatenate to do it:

from collections.abc import Callable
from typing import Concatenate


def requires_int[**P, R](func: Callable[Concatenate[int, str, P], R]) -> Callable[Concatenate[int, str, P], R]:
    return func

def foo(bar: int, baz: str, quz: bool) -> None:
    return None

def spam(quz: bool) -> None:
    return None


reveal_type(requires_int(foo)) # (int, str, quz: bool) -> None
requires_int(spam) # Error

Callable Protocol

ParamSpec can preserve arbitrary named arguments, but it doesn't let you specify the names. For that, you can't use a Callable at all. Instead, you can define a custom Protocol with a __call__ method:

from typing import Protocol


class FooLike(Protocol):
    def __call__(self, bar: int) -> None:
        ...

def foo(bar: int) -> None:
    return None

def spam(ham: int) -> None:
    return None


a: FooLike = foo
b: FooLike = spam # Positional parameter name mismatch: got `ham`, want `bar`

All messages come from the Pyrefly sandbox.

Q: How can I access official Apache website? A:

100% packet loss from ping doesn't necessarily mean the Apache website is down. Many web servers simply block ICMP ping requests.

Since Maven and Tomcat are also not loading, I'd check DNS and HTTPS separately. Try nslookup maven.apache.org and curl -I https://maven.apache.org. If both fail, the problem is more likely your network, DNS, proxy, or firewall.

Q: How can I support Google Sign-In for arbitrary websites in an iOS WKWebView-based browser? A:

For an iOS WKWebView browser, Google Sign-In can be tricky because Google may block authentication flows inside embedded webviews. A better approach is to open the Google login flow using ASWebAuthenticationSession or the system browser, then return the authentication result to your app. This is generally more reliable and follows Apple's authentication rules better than trying to force Google login directly inside WKWebView.

Q: How to "hide" chrome extension local storage A:

You can try abusing chrome.alarms API:

  1. create an alarm in a year's time, for example, give it a name that is JSON.stringify() of your data. If you'll reach some internal length limit you can make many of these distant alarms. And if your data is extremely big but is repetitive and thus compressible, use some lz or zip library to pack it, then convert to base64 string and use it as an alarm name.
  2. to get the data use chrome.alarms.getAll

I suppose this won't survive temporary disabling of the extension, but you should use those other standard methods for redundancy, and use whichever survives to restore the cleared ones.

P.S. Chrome 150 and newer limit the name to 1024 characters: https://crbug.com/445720439.

Q: How to make this stream gatherer threadsafe? A:

Your understanding is incorrect. You do not need to synchronize Holder. The Stream / Gatherer implementation does not lock get/set either. It never shares one Holder across threads.

That is why a parallel run still finds the max.

Parallel gatherers isolate state; they do not synchronize it

Gatherer.of(...) is parallelizable because you supplied a real combiner. On a parallel stream the pipeline does this:

  1. Split the source into partitions.

  2. Call the initializer once per partition. Each worker gets its own Holder.

  3. Run the integrator only against that partition's Holder.

  4. After both partitions finish integrating, call the combiner to merge the two holders.

  5. Call the finisher once on the final merged state.

The Gatherer javadoc requires that partitions are processed in isolation, combining happens only after integration is complete for both partitions, and once a state object is passed to the combiner or finisher it is never passed back to the integrator.

So thread A never calls set on thread B's Holder. Isolation is not the same as synchronization.

This is the same model as a non-concurrent Collector. Collectors.toList() uses a plain ArrayList on parallel streams for the same reason: each partition has its own list; the combiner concatenates them later.

Each thread computes a local max. The combiner then picks the larger of the two local maxes. That is ordinary parallel reduction, not a race on one shared box.

partition 1: Holder(12) + partition 2: Holder(99)

                      |

               combiner -\> Holder(99)

                      |

               finisher -\> push(99)

Why Holder looking "unsafe" does not matter

This would be a data race:

Holder<Integer> shared = new Holder<>();

Gatherer.of(() -> shared, ...); // every partition mutates the SAME object

Your initializer is:

() -> new Holder<Integer>()

Each partition gets a new instance. get/set are not concurrent on that instance, so adding synchronized would only add overhead.

parallel() after gather() still parallelizes the gatherer. The last parallel() / sequential() before the terminal operation sets the mode for the whole pipeline:

al.stream().gather(maxer).parallel().forEach(System.out::println);

// same evaluation mode as

al.parallelStream().gather(maxer).forEach(System.out::println);

So the gatherer is running in parallel. It still works because state is partition-local, not because the JDK locks Holder.

The real bugs

The gatherer is already thread-safe and still incorrect on some inputs.

The combiner NPEs on an empty partition:

(state1, state2) -> state1.get() > state2.get() ? state1 : state2

An empty split leaves Holder.t == null. The > operator unboxes Integer and throws NullPointerException.

Parallel splits of a 100,000-element ArrayList are usually non-empty, so this test hides the bug. Smaller lists, a filter, or an unlucky split can hit it.

The finisher on an empty stream:

(state, ds) -> ds.push(state.get());

If nothing was ever set, this pushes null.

The combiner is the only place two threads' results meet. It must treat "no value yet" as empty, not as a number.

Correct gatherer (still no locks)

Gatherer<Integer, Holder<Integer>, Integer> maxer = Gatherer.of(

    Holder::new,

    Gatherer.Integrator.ofGreedy((state, element, downstream) -\> {

        Integer current = state.get();

        if (current == null || current \< element) {

            state.set(element);

        }

        return true;

    }),

    (left, right) -\> {

        if (left.get() == null) return right;

        if (right.get() == null) return left;

        return left.get() \>= right.get() ? left : right;

    },

    (state, downstream) -\> {

        if (state.get() != null) {

            downstream.push(state.get());

        }

    }

);

al.parallelStream().gather(maxer).forEach(System.out::println);

Integrator.ofGreedy is appropriate here because you never short-circuit, so the implementation does not need to inspect false on every element.

Use Gatherer.of(...) when you have an associative combiner. Use Gatherer.ofSequential(...) only when the operation cannot be split (windows, running totals). Sequential gatherers use defaultCombiner() and stay sequential even if you call parallel().

When you would need thread safety

  • The initializer returns a shared object (static, captured local, singleton).

  • The integrator / combiner / finisher mutates some other shared field, list, or map.

  • You keep a Downstream or state reference and use it after the callback returns (the javadoc forbids that).

None of those apply to a per-partition Holder.

Bottom line: do not make this gatherer thread-safe by synchronizing Holder. The framework already confines each state object to one thread during integration. Your job is a combiner that merges two finished local maxes and handles empty partitions. The experiment "it found the max without synchronized, so either I am wrong or the JDK locks state" — you were wrong about sharing. The JDK isolates state; it does not lock it.

Q: Azure DevOps nuget restore fails with "Unable to find version 'x.x.x.x' of package" for internal feed package A:

The solution is to set the nuget version to 7.9.0.

Currently the actual version of nuget.

The solution in the YAML file looks like this:

- task: NuGetToolInstaller@1
    displayName: 'Use NuGet 7.9.0'
    inputs:
      versionSpec: 7.9.0
      checkLatest: true

Edit (August 19, 2026): I've also realized that running the build through Azure DevOps helps when switching from packages.config to PackageReference.
